reference.source: Nelson Textbook of Pediatrics / Ashcraft Pediatric Surgery
clinicalPearls: Malrotation is incomplete or abnormal rotation and fixation of the midgut, leaving a narrow mesenteric base that predisposes to catastrophic volvulus
Bilious vomiting in a previously well neonate or infant is midgut volvulus until proven otherwise and demands emergency evaluation
Ladd bands may cross and obstruct the duodenum even without volvulus, causing intermittent bilious vomiting
The upper gastrointestinal contrast study is the reference investigation, showing an abnormally positioned duodenojejunal junction and a corkscrew appearance of the proximal jejunum in volvulus
Ultrasound may reveal a whirlpool sign of the superior mesenteric vein wrapping around the artery and inversion of the normal superior mesenteric artery/vein relationship
Volvulus twists the bowel around the superior mesenteric vessels, threatening ischaemia and loss of the entire midgut within hours
Treatment of volvulus is urgent laparotomy with counterclockwise detorsion and a Ladd procedure to broaden the mesenteric base
reference.pathophysiology: During normal development the midgut herniates, rotates 270 degrees counterclockwise around the superior mesenteric artery, and returns to the abdomen with broad retroperitoneal fixation of the duodenojejunal junction and caecum. In malrotation this sequence is arrested or aberrant, so the mesenteric root remains narrow and points of fixation are abnormal, often with peritoneal (Ladd) bands tethering the caecum across the duodenum. The narrow pedicle allows the midgut to twist around the superior mesenteric vessels, producing both luminal obstruction and vascular compromise; sustained torsion leads to venous congestion, arterial occlusion, and infarction of bowel supplied by the superior mesenteric artery.
additionalDifferentials: Sepsis or metabolic disease causing bilious vomiting
additionalInvestigations: Upper gastrointestinal contrast study to define the position of the duodenojejunal junction and detect a corkscrew pattern
Abdominal ultrasound for the whirlpool sign and superior mesenteric artery/vein orientation
Abdominal radiograph, which may show a paucity of distal gas or a double-bubble-like proximal obstruction
Contrast enema to assess caecal position when other studies are equivocal
Blood gas and lactate to detect ischaemia and guide resuscitation
Baseline bloods and group-and-save in preparation for emergency surgery
redFlags: Bilious vomiting in a neonate or infant, mandating emergency assessment for volvulus
Abdominal distension with tenderness, guarding, or discoloration indicating ischaemia
Blood per rectum, a late and ominous sign of bowel infarction
Haemodynamic instability, acidosis, or rising lactate
Rapid clinical deterioration where imaging should not delay laparotomy
reference.prognosis: When volvulus is recognised and untwisted promptly the outcome is usually excellent, but delayed diagnosis can lead to massive bowel loss, short-bowel syndrome, or death. Elective Ladd procedure for asymptomatic malrotation carries low risk and prevents future volvulus.
pitfalls: Dismissing bilious vomiting as benign feed intolerance and delaying imaging or surgery
Awaiting non-urgent tests in a compromised infant instead of proceeding to laparotomy
Relying on a normal abdominal radiograph to exclude volvulus
Misinterpreting a normally positioned duodenojejunal junction variant and overlooking subtle malrotation
Failing to perform appendicectomy and full Ladd manoeuvres, leaving the patient at future risk
